title: Development of the Nervous System
summary: From neural plate to brain: how the nervous system is built and what goes wrong.

lessons.title: Neurulation & the Neural Crest

levels.kid:
Before you were born, you started as a tiny ball of cells. Very early, a flat strip of cells on your back side got busy building your brain and spinal cord.

The strip, called the **neural plate**, folded up like a taco. The edges came together and zipped closed into a tube, called the **neural tube**. The top of the tube grew into your brain. The rest became your spinal cord.

Some special cells at the edges of the taco wandered off on an adventure. They are called **neural crest** cells. They traveled all over the body and turned into lots of things: nerves in your skin and tummy, the color in your skin, and even some bones in your face!
levels.hs:
**Neurulation** is how the embryo builds its neural tube, the starting structure for the whole central nervous system. It happens very early, in the third and fourth weeks after conception, often before someone knows they are pregnant.

The steps:
1. The **notochord**, a rod of tissue along the embryo's midline, sends signals to the ectoderm (outer layer) above it.
2. That ectoderm thickens into the **neural plate**.
3. The plate's edges rise into **neural folds**, with a **neural groove** in the middle.
4. The folds meet and fuse into the **neural tube**, starting in the middle and zipping toward both ends. The front opening (anterior neuropore) closes around day 25 and the back opening (posterior neuropore) around day 27–28.

The neural tube becomes the brain and spinal cord. Its hollow center becomes the ventricles and the spinal canal.

**Neural crest cells** come from the edges of the folds. They migrate throughout the body and become:
- Sensory and autonomic ganglia (dorsal root ganglia, sympathetic chain)
- Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerves
- Melanocytes (skin pigment)
- The adrenal medulla
- Many bones and cartilage of the face and skull

If the tube does not close, babies can be born with neural tube defects like spina bifida. Taking folic acid before and during early pregnancy greatly lowers that risk.
levels.college:
**Induction**: the notochord and prechordal mesoderm induce overlying ectoderm to become neuroectoderm. Neural induction involves **inhibition of BMP signaling** by organizer-derived antagonists (noggin, chordin, follistatin): ectoderm "defaults" to neural fate when BMP is blocked.

**Dorsoventral patterning of the tube**
- Ventral: notochord and floor plate secrete **Sonic hedgehog (Shh)**, specifying motor neurons and ventral interneurons. This becomes the **basal plate** (motor).
- Dorsal: roof plate and overlying ectoderm secrete **BMPs and Wnts**, specifying sensory relay neurons. This becomes the **alar plate** (sensory).
- The **sulcus limitans** separates alar and basal plates, a boundary that persists in the brainstem: sensory nuclei lie lateral, motor nuclei medial, in the floor of the fourth ventricle.

**Closure**: primary neurulation forms the brain and spinal cord down to about the upper sacral level; **secondary neurulation** (canalization of the caudal eminence/tail bud) forms the conus medullaris and filum terminale. Closure begins at multiple points. Anterior neuropore closes ~day 25; posterior ~day 27–28.

**Neural crest** arises at the border between neural plate and surface ectoderm, undergoes an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrates. Derivatives include: dorsal root and cranial sensory ganglia, autonomic ganglia, enteric nervous system, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla chromaffin cells, leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid), odontoblasts, aorticopulmonary septum, and craniofacial skeleton.

**Placodes** (thickened surface ectoderm) contribute the lens, inner ear, olfactory epithelium and parts of cranial sensory ganglia.

**Clinical links**
- Neural crest disorders (neurocristopathies): Hirschsprung disease (absent enteric ganglia, distal colon), neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, DiGeorge-related conotruncal defects.
- Neural tube defects: anencephaly (anterior), spina bifida (posterior). Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and amniotic acetylcholinesterase suggest an open defect.
- Folic acid supplementation reduces NTD risk substantially; antiseizure drugs such as valproate raise it.
levels.phd:
Neural tube closure is a mechanical problem solved by coordinated cell behaviors, and defects are among the most common human birth defects (roughly 1 in 1,000 births, varying with folate fortification).

**Morphogenetic mechanics**
- **Convergent extension**: planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling (Vangl2, Celsr1, Scribble) narrows and elongates the neural plate. Mouse PCP mutants (e.g. loop-tail, Vangl2) develop **craniorachischisis**, an open neural tube from midbrain to spine, because a too-wide plate cannot close. PCP gene variants have been found in some human NTDs.
- **Hinge points**: the median hinge point (over the notochord, Shh-dependent) and dorsolateral hinge points (inhibited by Shh, promoted by noggin) bend the plate. In mice, dorsolateral hinge points are absent at upper spinal levels, where strong notochordal Shh suppresses them, but become essential at lower spinal levels, one reason closure defects are level-specific.
- **Apical constriction** via actomyosin (Shroom3) and interkinetic nuclear migration produce wedge-shaped cells.
- **Fusion**: non-neural ectoderm cells at the fold tips extend protrusions and adhere (ephrin/Eph, integrins); failure at this final step yields defects even with normal elevation.

**Folate and one-carbon metabolism**: folate supplies methyl groups and nucleotide synthesis for rapidly proliferating neuroepithelium. Yet most NTDs are not explained by low maternal folate, and folate-resistant forms exist (mouse curly tail responds to inositol rather than folate). MTHFR variants modestly raise risk. Valproate and carbamazepine, maternal diabetes, obesity and hyperthermia are established environmental risks.

**Neural crest biology**: crest cells are multipotent; lineage tracing in mice and zebrafish suggests many are individually multipotent while population-level fate depends on migratory route and local signals (e.g. dorsolateral route → melanocytes; ventromedial route → ganglia and Schwann cells). Cranial crest generates mesenchyme ("ectomesenchyme") forming bone and cartilage, an unusual ectodermal contribution to skeleton. **Schwann cell precursors** traveling along nerves turn out to be a second-wave source of melanocytes, parasympathetic neurons and enteric neurons, revising the classical picture.

**Secondary neurulation** in humans forms the caudal cord through cavitation of a mesenchymal cord; defects here produce closed (skin-covered) dysraphisms such as lipomyelomeningocele and tethered cord rather than open lesions.
levels.expert:
**Prenatal and neonatal practice**
- Screening: maternal serum AFP in the second trimester and detailed anatomy ultrasound. Cranial signs of open spina bifida include the "lemon sign" (frontal bone scalloping) and "banana sign" (cerebellum wrapped around the brainstem from Chiari II hindbrain herniation).
- The MOMS trial (2011) showed prenatal (fetal) repair of myelomeningocele reduced the need for shunting and improved motor outcomes at 30 months compared with postnatal repair, at the cost of higher prematurity and maternal uterine risks. Fetal surgery is now offered in selected centers.
- Postnatal myelomeningocele repair is usually performed within 24–72 hours to reduce infection risk. Keep the sac moist and covered, and position the baby prone.
- Latex precautions from birth: these patients have high rates of latex allergy.

**Associated problems the neurosurgeon follows for life**
- **Hydrocephalus** in most myelomeningocele patients; shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy with choroid plexus cauterization in selected infants.
- **Chiari II malformation**: symptomatic cases present with stridor, apnea, swallowing problems or weakness; first check that the shunt is working, because shunt failure can mimic or worsen hindbrain dysfunction.
- **Tethered cord**: new back pain, worsening gait, scoliosis progression, or bladder change in a growing child warrants evaluation. Nearly all repaired myelomeningoceles look tethered on MRI, so the decision is clinical.
- Neurogenic bladder (clean intermittent catheterization), bowel programs, orthopedic deformities.

**Occult (closed) spinal dysraphism**
- Cutaneous markers over the lumbosacral spine: hairy patch (hypertrichosis), subcutaneous lipoma, hemangioma, skin tag, dermal sinus tract above the gluteal crease. A simple low dimple within the gluteal cleft is usually benign.
- A dermal sinus can connect to the dura and cause recurrent meningitis; it should never be probed or injected.
- Early imaging (ultrasound in young infants before posterior elements ossify, MRI later) and prophylactic untethering of lipomas are debated topics.

**Neurocristopathies**: neuroblastoma (a common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, can present with opsoclonus-myoclonus); neurofibromatosis tumors arise from crest-derived Schwann lineage cells.

keyPoints: The notochord induces ectoderm to form the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube (weeks 3–4)
Anterior neuropore closes ~day 25; posterior ~day 27–28
Ventral Shh → basal plate (motor); dorsal BMP/Wnt → alar plate (sensory)
Neural crest makes DRG, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, facial bones
Folic acid lowers neural tube defect risk; valproate raises it

test.q: Which structure induces the overlying ectoderm to become the neural plate?
test.explain: The notochord signals (partly via BMP inhibition and Shh) to induce neuroectoderm.

test.q: Neural tube closure happens during which weeks of development?
test.explain: Neurulation occurs in weeks 3–4, often before pregnancy is recognized.

test.q: The hollow center of the neural tube becomes the ventricles and the spinal ___.
test.explain: The neural tube's lumen persists as the ventricular system and central canal.

test.q: Which is NOT a neural crest derivative?
test.explain: Oligodendrocytes come from the neural tube itself (CNS). The others are neural crest derived.

test.q: Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate specifies which region of the neural tube?
test.explain: Shh ventralizes the tube, producing motor neurons.

test.q: What vitamin taken before and during early pregnancy reduces neural tube defects?
test.explain: Folic acid supplementation substantially lowers NTD risk.

test.q: Failure of the anterior neuropore to close causes:
test.explain: Anterior closure failure leads to anencephaly; posterior failure leads to spina bifida.

test.q: The groove separating the alar and basal plates is the sulcus ___.
test.explain: The sulcus limitans divides sensory (alar, dorsal/lateral) from motor (basal, ventral/medial) territories.

test.q: Hirschsprung disease results from failed migration of neural crest cells to the:
test.explain: Absent enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon cause functional obstruction.

test.q: Elevated maternal serum AFP suggests:
test.explain: AFP leaks from open defects; amniotic acetylcholinesterase supports the diagnosis.

test.q: What is the name of the ectoderm-derived cells at the edges of the neural folds that migrate throughout the body? (two words)
test.explain: Neural crest cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and migrate widely.

test.q: Which antiseizure drug taken in pregnancy notably increases neural tube defect risk?
test.explain: Valproate carries the highest NTD and malformation risk among common antiseizure drugs.

kidTest.explain: The neural plate folds like a taco into a tube.

kidTest.q: The tube becomes your brain and...
kidTest.explain: The neural tube becomes brain and spinal cord.

kidTest.q: Neural crest cells are cells that...
kidTest.explain: They go on an adventure and become many things.

kidTest.q: What is the tube called that becomes the brain and spinal cord? (two words)
kidTest.explain: The neural tube is the start of the brain and spinal cord.

kidTest.q: Neural crest cells can turn into the color in your...
kidTest.explain: They become melanocytes, which make skin color.

kidTest.q: All of this happens...
kidTest.explain: It happens very early in the womb.

advancedTest.q: Mice with planar cell polarity mutations (e.g. Vangl2) develop an open neural tube from midbrain to spine (craniorachischisis) mainly because:
choices: Neural crest cells over-migrate and pull the neural folds apart
Failed convergent extension leaves the neural plate too wide to close
Folate receptors are missing, depriving the neural plate of folate
The notochord is absent, so no Shh signal induces the floor plate
advancedTest.explain: PCP-driven convergent extension narrows the plate; without it the folds cannot meet.

advancedTest.q: In the MOMS trial, prenatal myelomeningocele repair compared with postnatal repair:
choices: Reduced shunt need and improved motor outcomes but increased prematurity
Had no effect on hydrocephalus but improved bladder control in most
Reduced shunt need but worsened motor outcomes at 30 months
Lowered maternal risk while giving the same rate of preterm birth
advancedTest.explain: Fetal repair reduced shunting and improved motor function at 30 months, with more preterm birth and uterine complications.

advancedTest.q: A child with repaired myelomeningocele has new worsening gait and bladder function. Which is generally checked first?
choices: Shunt function, then clinical evaluation for tethering
Physical therapy alone, since decline is expected with growth
A spine X-ray to look for scoliosis first
A pituitary MRI for a hormonal cause
advancedTest.explain: Shunt malfunction can cause many neurological changes; tethering is a clinical diagnosis because repaired cords nearly always look tethered on MRI.

advancedTest.q: Which process forms the caudal spinal cord (conus and filum) from the tail bud by cavitation? (two words)
advancedTest.explain: Defects of secondary neurulation produce closed, skin-covered dysraphisms like lipomas and tethered cord.

lessons.title: Brain Vesicles & Their Adult Derivatives

levels.kid:
After the brain tube forms, its front end starts to puff up into bubbles, like blowing up balloons on a string.

First there are **three bubbles**: front, middle and back. Then the front and back bubbles split, so there are **five bubbles**.

Each bubble grows into a different part of your brain:
- The front one becomes the big thinking part, the **cerebrum**.
- The next one becomes the middle relay station, the **thalamus**.
- The middle one becomes the **midbrain**.
- The next becomes the **pons** and the **cerebellum**, which helps with balance.
- The last one becomes the **medulla**, which keeps you breathing.

The hollow insides of the bubbles turn into fluid-filled rooms called **ventricles**.
levels.hs:
Around week 4, the front of the neural tube swells into three **primary vesicles**:
1. **Prosencephalon** (forebrain)
2. **Mesencephalon** (midbrain)
3. **Rhombencephalon** (hindbrain)

By week 5, two of them split, giving five **secondary vesicles**:
- Prosencephalon → **telencephalon** and **diencephalon**
- Mesencephalon stays as the **mesencephalon**
- Rhombencephalon → **metencephalon** and **myelencephalon**

What each becomes in the adult:
- **Telencephalon**: cerebral hemispheres (cortex, white matter, basal ganglia). Its cavity becomes the **lateral ventricles**.
- **Diencephalon**: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (including the pineal gland) and the retina. Cavity: **third ventricle**.
- **Mesencephalon**: midbrain. Cavity: **cerebral aqueduct**.
- **Metencephalon**: pons and cerebellum. Cavity: upper part of the **fourth ventricle**.
- **Myelencephalon**: medulla oblongata. Cavity: lower part of the fourth ventricle.

The rest of the tube becomes the spinal cord, with its central canal.

A good memory trick: the names go in order front to back, and the word "encephalon" means "brain." So telencephalon is the "end brain," diencephalon the "between brain," and myelencephalon the "marrow brain" (it continues into the spinal cord). The eye's retina is actually an outgrowth of the brain, which is why doctors can see brain-related problems when they look in your eyes.
levels.college:
**Flexures**: as vesicles form, the tube bends. The **cephalic (mesencephalic) flexure** at the midbrain and the **cervical flexure** at the hindbrain–spinal cord junction are ventral bends; the **pontine flexure** bends the opposite way, splaying the hindbrain open so the alar plates move lateral to the basal plates. That is why, in the medulla and pons, sensory nuclei sit lateral to motor nuclei on the floor of the fourth ventricle instead of dorsal to them.

**Vesicle → adult derivative → cavity**
- Telencephalon → cerebral cortex, basal ganglia (striatum, globus pallidus), hippocampus, amygdala, olfactory bulbs → lateral ventricles (connected to the third through the interventricular foramina of Monro).
- Diencephalon → thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (pineal, habenula), subthalamus, posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis), optic vesicle → retina and optic nerve → third ventricle.
- Mesencephalon → tectum (superior and inferior colliculi), tegmentum, cerebral peduncles → cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius).
- Metencephalon → pons, cerebellum → upper fourth ventricle.
- Myelencephalon → medulla → lower fourth ventricle → central canal.

**Pituitary**: the posterior pituitary is a downgrowth of the diencephalon (infundibulum); the anterior pituitary comes from **Rathke's pouch**, an upgrowth of oral ectoderm. Remnants of Rathke's pouch give rise to **craniopharyngiomas**.

**Segmentation**: the hindbrain is transiently divided into **rhombomeres**, specified by Hox genes, and each pair relates to particular cranial nerve nuclei and pharyngeal arches. The midbrain–hindbrain boundary (isthmic organizer, FGF8) patterns the midbrain and cerebellum.

**Cortex expansion**: the telencephalon grows enormously, arching back over the diencephalon in a C shape. That arc explains why the lateral ventricle, caudate nucleus, hippocampus/fornix and stria terminalis all follow C-shaped courses, with the temporal lobe swinging down and forward.

**CSF pathway** follows directly: lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Magendie (median) and Luschka (lateral) → subarachnoid space.
levels.phd:
Regional identity along the neuraxis is laid down by **signaling centers** and **transcription factor codes**, and the vesicle stage is the morphological readout of this patterning.

**Anteroposterior patterning**: an early "activation–transformation" scheme (Nieuwkoop) proposes that neural tissue is initially anterior, then posteriorized by Wnt, FGF and retinoic acid gradients. Head organizer tissues (anterior visceral endoderm, anterior neural ridge) secrete Wnt antagonists (Dkk1) to protect forebrain identity. Transcription factors partition domains: Otx2 (forebrain/midbrain) abuts Gbx2 (hindbrain) at the midbrain–hindbrain boundary, where mutual repression positions the **isthmic organizer** expressing FGF8 and Wnt1. FGF8 beads ectopically placed in the diencephalon can induce midbrain or cerebellar structures, demonstrating organizer activity.

**Forebrain organizers**: the anterior neural ridge (FGF8) patterns the telencephalon; the cortical hem (Wnts and BMPs) induces the hippocampus; the antihem; and the **zona limitans intrathalamica** (Shh) separating prethalamus from thalamus. Diencephalic segmentation is described by the **prosomeric model** (Puelles and Rubenstein), which reinterprets the forebrain as a series of transverse segments along a curved axis. Under this model the hypothalamus is rostral (secondary prosencephalon) rather than part of the diencephalon proper, a departure from the classical columnar scheme still used in clinical teaching.

**Rhombomeres and Hox codes**: rhombomeres r1–r8 are compartments with cell-lineage restriction (Eph–ephrin boundaries). Nested Hox expression (Hoxa1, Hoxb1, Hoxa2, etc.) specifies segmental identity; for instance, Hoxb1 in r4 specifies facial motor neurons, whose cell bodies then migrate caudally to r6 while their axons loop around the abducens nucleus, producing the **internal genu of the facial nerve** and the facial colliculus. Hoxa1 mutations cause Bosley–Salih–Alorainy and Athabascan brainstem dysgenesis syndromes with horizontal gaze palsy, deafness and cardiovascular anomalies.

**Cerebellar origin**: the cerebellum derives from r1 alar plate (the "upper rhombic lip" giving granule cell precursors that migrate over the surface as the external granular layer) and the ventricular zone (Purkinje cells, GABAergic). Granule neuron precursor proliferation driven by Purkinje-derived Shh links development to the SHH subgroup of medulloblastoma.
levels.expert:
Embryology is the logic behind much of pediatric neurosurgery and many imaging findings.

**Holoprosencephaly**: failure of the prosencephalon to divide into two hemispheres. Spectrum: alobar (single ventricle, fused thalami), semilobar, lobar. Associated with midline facial anomalies (cyclopia, single central incisor, hypotelorism) because forebrain and face share Shh-dependent patterning. Causes include SHH mutations, trisomy 13, maternal diabetes and cholesterol synthesis defects (Smith–Lemli–Opitz, since Shh signaling requires cholesterol). "The face predicts the brain."

**Septo-optic dysplasia**: absent septum pellucidum, optic nerve hypoplasia and pituitary dysfunction; screen endocrine function because adrenal insufficiency or growth hormone deficiency can be life-threatening or missed.

**Craniopharyngioma**: a Rathke's pouch remnant tumor. Adamantinomatous (children; calcified, cystic with "machinery oil" fluid, CTNNB1 mutation) versus papillary (adults; BRAF V600E, which opens targeted therapy options). Presents with visual field loss (bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression), endocrine failure, hydrocephalus. Surgery near the hypothalamus risks obesity, diabetes insipidus and memory problems, so many surgeons aim for hypothalamus-sparing resection plus radiotherapy rather than radical removal.

**Dandy–Walker malformation** (a fourth ventricle/hindbrain development disorder): cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle, vermian hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa with elevated torcula. Hydrocephalus often needs shunting, sometimes of both the lateral ventricles and the cyst.

**Chiari malformations**: Chiari I is cerebellar tonsillar descent (often 5 mm or more below the foramen magnum) with an often normal-sized posterior fossa, sometimes with syringomyelia, presenting with cough-induced occipital headache. Chiari II involves the vermis and brainstem and is nearly always associated with myelomeningocele.

**Imaging pearls**
- The C-shaped arc of telencephalic structures means a temporal horn lesion and a caudate lesion can be part of one continuous process along the ventricle.
- Pineal region masses (diencephalic epithalamus) compress the dorsal midbrain and aqueduct, causing **Parinaud syndrome** (upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus) and obstructive hydrocephalus.
- Aqueductal stenosis enlarges lateral and third ventricles but leaves the fourth normal: ideal anatomy for endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

keyPoints: Primary vesicles: prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon
Secondary: telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon
Telencephalon → cerebral hemispheres/lateral ventricles; diencephalon → thalamus, hypothalamus, retina/third ventricle
Mesencephalon → midbrain/aqueduct; metencephalon → pons + cerebellum; myelencephalon → medulla
Anterior pituitary comes from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm); posterior from diencephalon

Facial motor neurons born in rhombomere 4 migrate caudally, dragging their axons around the abducens nucleus
The facial nerve develops from migrating neural crest that wraps around nearby nuclei

lessons.title: Neurogenesis, Migration & Axon Guidance

levels.kid:
Building a brain is like building a giant city.

First, the brain makes billions of new nerve cells. This is called **neurogenesis**. New cells are made near the middle of the brain, next to the fluid rooms.

Next, the new cells have to travel to where they belong, like people moving into their new houses. Many climb up long ropes made by helper cells, like climbing a ladder to the top floors. This is called **migration**.

Then each nerve cell grows a long wire to connect with other cells. The tip of the wire sniffs around, following "come here" and "go away" smells, until it finds the right partner. This is **axon guidance**.

When this goes wrong, the brain can be wired or built in the wrong shape.
levels.hs:
The nervous system develops in a set order: make the neurons, move them, connect them, then trim the connections.

**1. Neurogenesis**
Neural stem cells line the inside of the neural tube in the **ventricular zone**. They divide many times. In the cortex, a special stem cell type, the **radial glial cell**, both makes neurons and acts as a scaffold. Most neurons are made before birth.

**2. Migration**
New neurons travel outward from the ventricles.
- Many cortical neurons climb along radial glial fibers (**radial migration**).
- The cortex is built **inside-out**: the earliest neurons form the deepest layer (layer 6) and later neurons climb past them to form the upper layers.
- Inhibitory interneurons are born elsewhere (in the ganglionic eminences of the developing basal ganglia) and travel sideways into the cortex (**tangential migration**).

**3. Axon guidance**
Each young neuron sends out an axon tipped with a **growth cone**, a hand-like structure that senses chemical cues. Some cues attract (netrin can), some repel (Slit, semaphorins), some work by contact, and others diffuse from a distance.

**4. Synapse formation and pruning**
Neurons make too many connections, then remove the unused ones. About half of some neuron populations die during development (programmed cell death), depending on whether they get enough growth factor from their targets. This "use it or lose it" pruning continues through the teenage years, especially in the prefrontal cortex.
levels.college:
**Neurogenesis**
- Neuroepithelial cells divide symmetrically to expand the pool, then transform into **radial glia**, which divide asymmetrically: one daughter stays a stem cell, the other becomes a neuron or an **intermediate progenitor** (in the subventricular zone) that amplifies output.
- **Interkinetic nuclear migration**: progenitor nuclei move between the apical (ventricular) surface, where mitosis occurs, and basal positions during S phase.
- **Notch–Delta lateral inhibition** maintains progenitors; proneural bHLH genes (Neurog2, Ascl1) drive neuronal differentiation.
- In primates, an expanded **outer subventricular zone** with outer radial glia contributes to cortical expansion and folding.

**Migration**
- Radial migration (excitatory neurons): locomotion along radial glia and somal translocation. Reelin from **Cajal–Retzius cells** in the marginal zone signals the inside-out stacking; reeler mice have inverted layers.
- Tangential migration (GABAergic interneurons) from the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences.
- Key migration molecules: LIS1 and doublecortin (DCX) regulate microtubules and dynein-based nucleokinesis; filamin A (FLNA) regulates actin.
- Cerebellar granule cells migrate inward from the external granular layer along Bergmann glia.

**Axon guidance**
- Growth cones contain actin-rich filopodia and lamellipodia; cue receptors regulate actin polymerization via Rho GTPases.
- Four classic families: **netrins** (DCC receptors attract; UNC5 receptors repel), **Slits** (Robo receptors repel), **semaphorins** (plexins/neuropilins; mostly repel), **ephrins** (Eph receptors; contact-dependent, topographic maps like the retinotectal projection).
- **Midline crossing**: commissural axons in the spinal cord are attracted to the floor plate by netrin and Shh. Before crossing, Robo3 suppresses Slit repulsion; after crossing, Robo1/2 is upregulated, so axons are expelled and do not recross.

**Survival and refinement**
- **Neurotrophic hypothesis** (Levi-Montalcini, Hamburger): neurons compete for limited target-derived factors (NGF, BDNF, NT-3). Losers undergo apoptosis.
- Activity-dependent refinement: Hubel and Wiesel showed that monocular deprivation during a critical period shifts ocular dominance columns, producing permanent amblyopia if uncorrected.
- Myelination continues into the third decade; prefrontal synaptic pruning extends through adolescence.
levels.phd:
**Temporal patterning**: radial glia progress through a sequence of competence states, generating deep-layer neurons first and upper-layer neurons later. Heterochronic transplantation shows early progenitors can produce late fates when placed in older environments, but late progenitors cannot revert, suggesting progressive restriction (McConnell; more recent work shows partial reversibility via Foxg1 and other regulators). Recent single-cell work identifies conserved temporal transcription factor cascades, analogous to Drosophila neuroblast temporal identity, though the mammalian mechanism is less linear.

**Human-specific expansion**: outer radial glia (oRG) in the outer SVZ have a basal process but no apical attachment, divide via "mitotic somal translocation", and generate large numbers of upper-layer neurons. Human-specific genes (e.g. NOTCH2NL, ARHGAP11B) increase basal progenitor proliferation; ARHGAP11B expression in mouse or ferret increases folding. Cortical folding mechanics combine differential tangential expansion with tissue mechanics, with gyrification index predicted by oRG abundance.

**Migration mechanics**: nucleokinesis requires a perinuclear cage of microtubules pulled by dynein, with LIS1 regulating dynein processivity. Doublecortin bundles microtubules. Reelin binds VLDLR and ApoER2, triggering Dab1 phosphorylation by Src-family kinases, which promotes terminal somal translocation and detachment from radial glia at the top of the cortical plate. Reelin also signals at adult synapses, modulating NMDA receptor function.

**Guidance computation**: growth cones show adaptation, resetting sensitivity after exposure to a gradient (via desensitization and resensitization involving local protein synthesis), allowing them to navigate over orders-of-magnitude concentration ranges. The same cue can attract or repel depending on intracellular cAMP/cGMP and Ca2+ levels (Ming and Poo), and receptor switching at intermediate targets (Robo3 splice isoforms, Robo3.1 versus Robo3.2) gates midline behavior. Axon tract formation also uses pioneer axons and fasciculation, and selective "axon degeneration" programs (SARM1-dependent) prune exuberant projections.

**Critical periods** are opened by maturation of parvalbumin interneurons (triggered partly by Otx2 transfer from the retina/choroid plexus) and closed by perineuronal nets and myelin-associated inhibitors (Nogo receptor, Lynx1). Digesting perineuronal nets with chondroitinase ABC can reopen plasticity in adult animals, research relevant to amblyopia and spinal cord injury repair.
levels.expert:
**Clinical correlates of migration and connectivity errors**
- **Lissencephaly** ("smooth brain"): LIS1 (PAFAH1B1) deletions (posterior-predominant, Miller–Dieker syndrome with 17p13.3 deletion and facial dysmorphism) and DCX mutations (anterior-predominant in males). Presents with severe developmental delay, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and infantile spasms.
- **Subcortical band heterotopia** ("double cortex"): usually females heterozygous for X-linked DCX, often with epilepsy and milder intellectual disability.
- **Periventricular nodular heterotopia**: FLNA mutations in females; neurons never left the ventricular zone. Often presents as epilepsy in adolescence with normal intelligence. Associated with cardiovascular and connective tissue problems.
- **Polymicrogyria**: excessive small gyri, from postmigrational disorganization (genetic or acquired, e.g. congenital CMV). Perisylvian polymicrogyria causes oromotor dysfunction and epilepsy.
- **Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD)**: a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy in children; FCD type II involves dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells, often from somatic mTOR pathway mutations. MRI signs: blurring of the gray–white junction and the "transmantle sign." It is highly surgically curable when completely resected.
- **Tuberous sclerosis**: TSC1/TSC2 mutations (mTOR overactivation) cause cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGA) near the foramen of Monro, which can cause hydrocephalus. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink SEGAs and reduce seizures.
- **Agenesis of the corpus callosum**: commissural guidance failure. MRI shows parallel lateral ventricles and Probst bundles (axons that failed to cross and run front to back). Can be isolated and mild or part of syndromes.

**Epilepsy surgery evaluation** often comes down to finding a developmental lesion: high-resolution 3T MRI, PET, MEG and stereo-EEG. Complete resection of a lesion like FCD or a heterotopia-related focus offers seizure-freedom rates far higher than adding more drugs after two have failed.

**Regeneration**: adult CNS axons regenerate poorly because of inhibitory myelin proteins (Nogo-A, MAG, OMgp), the glial scar's chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, and reduced intrinsic growth programs (PTEN/mTOR). These are targets in spinal cord injury trials, an area where developmental neuroscience directly guides neurosurgical research.

keyPoints: Neurons are born in the ventricular zone from radial glia; radial glia also act as migration scaffolds
Cortex forms inside-out: early neurons deep (layer 6), later neurons superficial; reelin from Cajal–Retzius cells guides this
Interneurons migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences
Growth cones follow cues: netrin (attract via DCC), Slit/Robo (repel), semaphorins, ephrins
Neurons compete for neurotrophic factors; unused connections are pruned

test.q: Where are most new neurons generated in the developing cortex?
test.explain: Progenitors lining the ventricles (ventricular and subventricular zones) generate neurons.

test.q: The cerebral cortex is built 'inside-out,' meaning:
choices: Neurons are born at the surface and migrate inward to the ventricle
The six layers are generated at the same time and then sort out
Early-born neurons form the surface layer; later ones sit beneath them
Early-born neurons form deep layers; later ones pass them to form superficial layers
test.explain: Later neurons migrate past earlier ones, so layer 6 forms first and layers 2–3 last.

test.q: New cortical neurons climb along the fibers of radial ___ cells.
test.explain: Radial glia are both progenitors and migration scaffolds.

test.q: Cortical inhibitory interneurons mainly reach the cortex by:
choices: Radial migration from the cortical ventricular zone
Tangential migration from the ganglionic eminences
test.explain: GABAergic interneurons arise in the ventral telencephalon and migrate sideways.

test.q: What is the hand-like tip of a growing axon called? (two words)
test.explain: The growth cone senses guidance cues and steers the axon.

test.q: Which secreted protein from Cajal–Retzius cells is needed for normal cortical layering?
test.explain: Reelin deficiency (reeler mice) produces roughly inverted cortical layers.

test.q: Slit proteins acting on Robo receptors typically:
test.explain: Slit–Robo signaling is repulsive and helps stop axons from recrossing the midline.

test.q: According to the neurotrophic hypothesis, neurons compete for limited target-derived factors such as nerve growth ___ (NGF).
test.explain: Neurons that fail to get enough trophic factor die by apoptosis.

test.q: Netrin attracts commissural axons through which receptor?
test.explain: Netrin attracts via DCC; it repels via UNC5 receptors.

test.q: Mutations in LIS1 or doublecortin cause which disorder of neuronal migration?
test.explain: Impaired microtubule-based migration produces a smooth brain with few gyri.

test.q: What is the term for removing unused synapses during development, continuing through adolescence?
test.explain: Synaptic pruning refines circuits; prefrontal pruning extends into the teenage years.

test.q: Hubel and Wiesel found that covering one eye during a critical period causes:
choices: Stronger cortical responses to the covered eye when it reopens
Faster growth of the covered eye and longer axial length
No lasting change once the eye is uncovered again
Permanent loss of cortical responses to that eye
test.explain: Ocular dominance shifts toward the open eye; uncorrected, this is amblyopia.

kidTest.q: Making new nerve cells is called...
kidTest.explain: Neurogenesis means making new neurons.

kidTest.q: New brain cells travel to their homes by climbing...
kidTest.explain: They climb along radial glia like ladders.

kidTest.q: The tip of a growing nerve wire finds its partner by...
choices: Waiting for a bus to drive it there
kidTest.explain: Chemical cues attract or repel the growing tip.

kidTest.q: What is it called when new brain cells travel to where they belong?
kidTest.explain: Migration means moving to the right place.

kidTest.q: Building a brain is like building a...
kidTest.explain: Cells are made, moved into place and connected.

kidTest.q: Unused connections in the brain get...
kidTest.explain: Use it or lose it: unused links are pruned.

advancedTest.q: A teen girl with normal intelligence has new focal seizures; MRI shows nodules of gray matter lining the lateral ventricles. The most likely gene?
advancedTest.explain: Periventricular nodular heterotopia is classically X-linked FLNA, mostly in females; neurons failed to leave the ventricular zone.

advancedTest.q: Commissural spinal axons cross the midline once and never recross mainly because:
choices: Netrin disappears after birth, so nothing attracts them back to the midline
After crossing they upregulate Robo1/2 and become sensitive to Slit repulsion
They lose their growth cones permanently once they cross the floor plate
Myelin wraps axons right after crossing, stopping growth-cone turns
advancedTest.explain: Robo3 silences Slit repulsion before crossing; after crossing Robo1/2 dominate and expel axons from the midline.

advancedTest.q: A child with drug-resistant focal epilepsy has MRI showing gray–white blurring and a transmantle sign. Best next step in management thinking:
choices: Epilepsy surgery evaluation for likely focal cortical dysplasia type II
Ignore the imaging; these MRI findings are a common normal variant
Corpus callosotomy as the first-choice curative operation for this lesion
Add a fourth antiseizure drug indefinitely and repeat MRI in five years
advancedTest.explain: FCD II is often curable with complete resection; after two failed appropriate drugs, surgical evaluation is indicated.

advancedTest.q: Which adult-CNS myelin protein (two parts, e.g. Nogo-?) is a major inhibitor of axon regeneration?
advancedTest.explain: Nogo-A, MAG and OMgp signal through Nogo receptor complexes to collapse growth cones, limiting CNS regeneration.

lessons.title: Developmental Malformations

levels.kid:
Sometimes, while a baby is growing inside its mom, a step in building the brain or spine doesn't finish quite right.

- If the spine tube doesn't zip all the way closed, a baby can be born with a bump on its back. That is called **spina bifida**.
- If the back of the brain is squished down into the neck, it is called a **Chiari** problem.
- If fluid can't drain from the brain's rooms, the head fills up with too much fluid. That is **hydrocephalus**.

Doctors can find many of these before a baby is born with special pictures. Brain surgeons can fix or help many of them, like closing the back or putting in a tiny drain tube.

Moms taking a vitamin called folic acid helps prevent some of these problems.
levels.hs:
Malformations happen when a step of development goes wrong.

**Neural tube defects (failed closure, weeks 3–4)**
- **Anencephaly**: the top of the neural tube fails to close; most of the brain and skull do not form. Fatal.
- **Encephalocele**: brain tissue pushes out through a skull defect, often at the back of the head.
- **Spina bifida occulta**: a small gap in the vertebrae, often with only a tuft of hair or dimple on the skin; usually harmless.
- **Meningocele**: the meninges bulge out through the gap; nerves usually stay in place.
- **Myelomeningocele**: the spinal cord and nerves bulge out in an open sac. This causes leg weakness, bladder and bowel problems, and usually comes with hydrocephalus and a Chiari II malformation.

**Hindbrain malformations**
- **Chiari I**: the cerebellar tonsils sit too low, through the foramen magnum. May cause headaches worsened by coughing.
- **Chiari II**: more of the hindbrain is pushed down; seen with myelomeningocele.
- **Dandy–Walker**: an underdeveloped cerebellar vermis and a big cyst-like fourth ventricle.

**Forebrain and size problems**
- **Holoprosencephaly**: the forebrain fails to split into two halves.
- **Microcephaly**: a very small head and brain, from genetic causes or infections like Zika virus.

**Hydrocephalus** is a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid, often because a narrow passage like the cerebral aqueduct is blocked. Neurosurgeons treat it with a shunt (a tube draining fluid to the abdomen) or by making a new opening inside the brain (endoscopic third ventriculostomy).
levels.college:
Organizing malformations by developmental stage aids diagnosis.

**Dorsal induction (neurulation, weeks 3–4)**
- Open defects: anencephaly, craniorachischisis, myelomeningocele (most commonly lumbosacral). AFP elevated.
- Closed (skin-covered) dysraphisms: lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus tract, split cord malformation (diastematomyelia), tight filum terminale, all of which can tether the cord.
- Encephaloceles: occipital common in Western populations; frontoethmoidal more common in Southeast Asia.

**Ventral induction (weeks 5–10)**
- Holoprosencephaly spectrum (SHH pathway); septo-optic dysplasia.
- Dandy–Walker malformation: vermian hypoplasia rotated upward, cystic fourth ventricle, enlarged posterior fossa with elevated tentorium and torcular herophili. Distinguish from mega cisterna magna and Blake's pouch cyst.

**Proliferation**: microcephaly (primary genetic forms affect centrosomal genes such as ASPM and MCPH1; congenital Zika and CMV infection); megalencephaly (e.g. PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway mutations); hemimegalencephaly, a cause of catastrophic infant epilepsy.

**Migration**: lissencephaly, subcortical band and periventricular heterotopia, cobblestone malformations (dystroglycanopathies with muscle and eye involvement, e.g. Walker–Warburg).

**Organization**: polymicrogyria, schizencephaly (gray-matter-lined cleft from ventricle to surface; "open lip" or "closed lip"), focal cortical dysplasia.

**Hindbrain herniation**
- **Chiari I**: tonsillar descent (classically 5 mm or more below the foramen magnum in adults), small posterior fossa; syringomyelia in a minority, causing cape-like loss of pain and temperature. Symptomatic cases: Valsalva/cough occipital headache, lower cranial nerve signs.
- **Chiari II**: vermis, fourth ventricle and medulla displaced, tectal beaking, nearly always with myelomeningocele.

**Destructive vs malformative**: **hydranencephaly** (hemispheres replaced by CSF after a vascular insult such as bilateral ICA occlusion, with intact thalami and posterior fossa) differs from severe hydrocephalus, where a thin cortical mantle remains; this distinction affects shunting decisions.

**Hydrocephalus in infants**: enlarging head circumference crossing percentiles, bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, "sunsetting" eyes (upgaze palsy from dorsal midbrain pressure), irritability and vomiting.
levels.phd:
Malformations are natural experiments that reveal developmental mechanisms, and modern genetics has reclassified many by pathway rather than morphology.

**mTORopathies**: hemimegalencephaly, focal cortical dysplasia type II, tuberous sclerosis and some megalencephaly syndromes share PI3K–AKT–mTOR hyperactivation. Somatic mosaic mutations (e.g. in MTOR, PIK3CA, AKT3, DEPDC5 with a second hit) arising in a progenitor produce a lesion whose size reflects when and in which lineage the mutation arose: earlier, larger. Detection required deep sequencing of resected tissue; cell-free DNA from CSF is being explored. This paradigm links malformation, epileptogenesis and potential targeted therapy (mTOR inhibitors).

**Ciliopathies**: primary cilia transduce Shh signaling. Joubert syndrome (molar tooth sign from thick, horizontal superior cerebellar peduncles and a deep interpeduncular fossa, with vermian hypoplasia) and Meckel–Gruber syndrome (occipital encephalocele, polydactyly, cystic kidneys) arise from mutations in ciliary transition-zone proteins, linking neural patterning to kidney and retinal disease.

**Microcephaly and the centrosome**: MCPH genes (ASPM, WDR62, CDK5RAP2, CENPJ) regulate spindle orientation and centriole duplication in radial glia. Defects push progenitors toward premature neurogenic (asymmetric) divisions, depleting the pool and shrinking the cortex while sparing architecture. Zika virus targets neural progenitors via entry factors (AXL implicated, though not required in all models) and triggers innate immune and apoptotic responses, producing severe microcephaly with calcifications, ventriculomegaly and arthrogryposis.

**Chiari I pathogenesis**: classically attributed to an underdeveloped occipital somite-derived posterior fossa (para-axial mesoderm), producing overcrowding. But tonsillar ectopia also arises secondarily from intracranial hypertension, intracranial hypotension (CSF leak, overshunting), craniosynostosis, and connective tissue laxity. Syrinx formation theories evolved from Gardner's "water hammer" to models where systolic pressure waves in the subarachnoid space, with the tonsils acting as pistons (Oldfield), drive CSF into the cord through perivascular spaces.

**Hydrocephalus genetics**: X-linked hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis (L1CAM mutations: adducted thumbs, spasticity, agenesis of the corpus callosum) shows that a cell adhesion molecule mediating axon guidance can produce a "plumbing" disorder. Motile ciliopathies of ependyma and choroid plexus disorders reveal CSF dynamics beyond simple obstruction, and the classical bulk-flow model is now supplemented by evidence for glymphatic and parenchymal fluid exchange.
levels.expert:
**Clinical decision-making in pediatric neurosurgery**

**Chiari I**
- Incidental tonsillar ectopia on MRI is common and often needs no surgery. Operate for symptoms clearly attributable to it (tussive occipital headache, brainstem or cranial nerve signs) or a significant or enlarging syrinx.
- Standard surgery: posterior fossa decompression (suboccipital craniectomy plus C1 laminectomy), with or without duraplasty. Duraplasty lowers reoperation rates but increases CSF-related complications (pseudomeningocele, aseptic meningitis); practice varies.
- Always exclude secondary causes first: a mass, hydrocephalus, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, or a CSF leak with intracranial hypotension (where decompression worsens things).

**Hydrocephalus**
- Ventriculoperitoneal shunt is the workhorse. Failure is common, with a substantial fraction failing within the first year or two. Shunt malfunction symptoms: headache, vomiting, lethargy, upgaze palsy, bradycardia and hypertension (Cushing response, a late and dangerous sign). Treat a lethargic child with a shunt as a shunt failure until proven otherwise.
- Shunt infection usually occurs within months of surgery, often from skin flora (Staphylococcus epidermidis).
- Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) works best for obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus such as aqueductal stenosis, and in older children. The ETV Success Score combines age, cause and prior shunt to estimate success. Adding choroid plexus cauterization (ETV/CPC) improves success in some infants.
- Slit ventricle syndrome and overdrainage are long-term shunt problems.

**Craniosynostosis** (premature suture fusion): sagittal (scaphocephaly, the most common), metopic (trigonocephaly), unicoronal (anterior plagiocephaly with a harlequin eye on X-ray), lambdoid (rare; distinguish from positional plagiocephaly, which shows a parallelogram head and is managed with repositioning or a helmet). Surgery: endoscopic strip craniectomy with helmeting in young infants or open cranial vault remodeling later. Syndromic forms (Crouzon, Apert: FGFR2 mutations) carry higher intracranial pressure risk.

**Encephalocele and myelomeningocele** repair aim: preserve neural tissue, achieve watertight dural closure, cover with healthy skin, and manage hydrocephalus. Multidisciplinary spina bifida clinics (urology, orthopedics, rehabilitation) make the biggest difference over a lifetime.

keyPoints: Myelomeningocele: open sac with cord and nerves; associated with hydrocephalus and Chiari II
Spina bifida occulta: bony defect only, often a hair tuft or dimple, usually harmless
Chiari I: low cerebellar tonsils; cough headache; may cause syringomyelia
Dandy–Walker: vermian hypoplasia plus cystic fourth ventricle and enlarged posterior fossa
Hydrocephalus is treated with a shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy (best for obstructive causes)

test.q: Which neural tube defect has the spinal cord and nerves protruding in an open sac?
test.explain: In myelomeningocele, neural tissue is in the sac; meningocele contains meninges and CSF only.

test.q: Spina bifida occulta is usually:
choices: Mild, sometimes marked only by a hair tuft or dimple
test.explain: It is a bony defect with intact skin and usually no symptoms.

test.q: In Chiari I malformation, which structures descend through the foramen magnum?
test.explain: Chiari I involves tonsillar descent; Chiari II involves vermis and brainstem too.

test.q: Chiari II malformation is nearly always associated with ___ (an open spinal defect).
test.explain: Chiari II and myelomeningocele occur together, often with hydrocephalus.

test.q: Dandy–Walker malformation features:
choices: Hypoplastic cerebellar vermis and cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle
Fused cerebral hemispheres with a single forebrain ventricle
Low cerebellar tonsils with a normal-sized posterior fossa
Smooth cortex with few gyri from failed neuronal migration
test.explain: Dandy–Walker is a hindbrain malformation with a large posterior fossa.

test.q: What is the term for excess CSF accumulation in the brain's ventricles?
test.explain: Hydrocephalus results from impaired CSF flow or absorption.

test.q: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy works best for hydrocephalus caused by:
choices: Absorption failure at the arachnoid granulations
test.explain: ETV bypasses an obstruction downstream of the third ventricle, so it suits obstructive causes like aqueductal stenosis.

test.q: Which infection in pregnancy is linked to severe congenital microcephaly?
test.explain: Zika infects neural progenitors, causing microcephaly with calcifications.

test.q: A syrinx associated with Chiari I classically causes cape-like loss of pain and ___ sensation.
test.explain: An expanding central cord cavity interrupts crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior commissure.

test.q: Holoprosencephaly is failure of the:
choices: Spinal cord to close at the lower end
Forebrain to divide into two hemispheres
Skull sutures to fuse at the right time
Cerebellum to form from the hindbrain
test.explain: The prosencephalon fails to cleave, often with midline facial anomalies.

test.q: What tube, draining CSF from a ventricle to the abdomen, is the most common hydrocephalus treatment? (abbreviation VP ...)
test.explain: A ventriculoperitoneal shunt diverts CSF to the peritoneal cavity for absorption.

test.q: A typical symptom of symptomatic Chiari I is:
choices: Frontal headache that eases when lying flat for a while
Sudden painless vision loss in one eye
Occipital headache worse with coughing or straining
test.explain: Valsalva maneuvers transiently worsen crowding at the foramen magnum.

kidTest.q: Spina bifida is when the spine tube...
choices: Is way too long for the back
Doesn't zip all the way closed
kidTest.explain: Part of the tube stays open.

kidTest.q: Too much fluid in the brain's rooms is called...
kidTest.explain: Hydrocephalus means extra fluid in the brain.

kidTest.q: Brain surgeons can help drain extra fluid with a...
kidTest.explain: A shunt is a tiny tube that drains fluid.

kidTest.q: Which vitamin helps prevent spina bifida? (two words)
kidTest.explain: Folic acid before and during early pregnancy helps prevent it.

kidTest.q: Doctors can often see these problems before birth with...
kidTest.explain: Ultrasound pictures show the baby inside.

kidTest.q: A Chiari problem is when the back of the brain is...
kidTest.explain: The cerebellum sits too low.

advancedTest.q: A 7-year-old with a VP shunt is lethargic, vomiting, and has a new upgaze palsy. Best working assumption:
advancedTest.explain: Signs of raised ICP in a shunted child mandate urgent evaluation (imaging, shunt series, neurosurgical review).

advancedTest.q: Before decompressing an asymptomatic-looking Chiari I in a patient with new orthostatic headaches, which secondary cause must be excluded because decompression could worsen it?
choices: Intracranial hypotension from a CSF leak
Migraine without aura, made worse by caffeine
advancedTest.explain: Low CSF pressure causes brain sag with tonsillar descent; treatment is to fix the leak, not decompress.

advancedTest.q: A newborn's CT shows hemispheres replaced by fluid with intact thalami, brainstem and cerebellum and no cortical mantle. This is:
choices: Hydranencephaly from a destructive vascular insult
advancedTest.explain: Hydranencephaly (often bilateral ICA territory destruction) lacks a cortical mantle, unlike hydrocephalus; prognosis and shunt goals differ.

advancedTest.q: A boy has hydrocephalus from aqueductal stenosis, adducted thumbs and spasticity. Which X-linked gene? (5 characters)
advancedTest.explain: L1CAM, a cell adhesion molecule for axon guidance, causes X-linked hydrocephalus (CRASH syndrome).
